item.title: International Feel: Highlights from Le Guess Who? 2026
item.dc:creator: Patrick Clarke
item.description:
Celebrating its 20th year, with a lineup focussed on bypassing arbitrary boundaries, Utrecht's flagship experimental festival forces even the most eclectic listener to go beyond, says Patrick Clarke

Bethlehem's Lawrence Sammour, photo by Maarten Mooijman

We start Le Guess Who? 2026 with Tortoise, who treat an enormous crowd to the cavernous Ronda space within Utrecht’s TivoliVredenburg complex. They offer a masterful display of how the subtlest shifts can produce the biggest effects, a tiny buzz of synth blooming slowly into something majestic and warm; a small nudge of bass snowballing until it’s an avalanche. Then, a trek up several flights of stairs to the much smaller Pandora, passing More Eaze as they soundcheck in a foyer, where the immensely charismatic Manaus-born musician...

item.title: Straight Hedge! Noel Gardner Reviews Punk & HC for November
item.dc:creator: Patrick Clarke
item.description:
From charge-the-enemy, knife-down-boot, shoelace-round-head hardcore to some gleaming and nasty Lima death rock, Noel Gardner's guide to the best in punk returns

Funeral, photo by Satanist Madness

Welcome (back) to what many are calling “the tersest column on the Quietus dot com”, not because of the windbag who writes it but on account of the belligerent barkers the windbag chooses to feature in it. Come lap up short songs of blunt aggression from bands with short names, the better to reflect the terseness in the presentation. 

Oakland’s Cell Rot have been at it for about a decade and get further away from hardcore generica with each release – while, significantly, never giving the impression they’re becoming bored of being a hardcore band. Their...

item.title: Claire Cronin – The Bruise
item.dc:creator: Robert Barry
item.description:
Claire Cronin

The Bruise

The folk horror Sandy Denny sees the horror of it all all too clearly

The Bruise by Claire Cronin

“Female singer songwriter” is a designation packed full of dated assumptions male singer songwriters have not had to contend with since the 60s. The category not only fails to illuminate, but flattens all difference, forcing artists who have very little in common to seem more similar than they are.

Claire Cronin is too touched by the uncanny to succumb to any such kookiness-at-all-costs shoehorning. Which isn’t to say The Bruise doesn’t have points of comparison, it’s just they are not Fiona Apple or Norah Jones, rather a folk horror Sandy Denny that cut her teeth on Twin Peaks and Carrie instead of...

item.title: A Hymn of Selfishness: Sheherazaad Interviewed
item.dc:creator: John Doran
item.description:
Khudgarzi is the debut album of Sheherazaad; the ghostly sound of female resistance in experimental pop and gothic folk. Words: Arusa Qureshi. Portraits: Zayira Ray

Khudgarzi by Sheherazaad

“There’s this fantastical, romanticised thing of being in grief and being dark and depressed, and then doing your best work,” American composer and theatre artist Sheherazaad tells me. A mere two months ago, she lost her grandmother, who was herself a music producer and, in many ways, the only other woman she knew who shared her intense, sometimes isolating relationship with music.
